extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematics; general problem-solvers interested in mathematical heuristics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and heuristics for solving mathematical problems (and for teaching them): how to vary and analyze problems, form and test conjectures, use proofs (complete and incomplete), and employ methods such as working backwards, analogy, and auxiliary constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary the problem by trying different standpoints and viewing the problem from different sides; success depends on choosing the right aspect — attacking the fortress from its accessible side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try changes to the data or viewpoint to discover which aspect is accessible. Example: change parameters (b→a or b→0) in the frustum problem to see limiting cases that suggest the final formula. Anti-pattern: repeating the exact same hopeless attempt (the 'insect' behavior) rather than exploring alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilization of formerly acquired knowledge via variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Varying the problem helps extract relevant elements from memory by creating new mental associations ('action by contact').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce new points/aspects to create contacts that recall previously learned facts and techniques; use variation to bring useful remembered elements into play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain intense concentration by changing the focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Intense concentration is required but fixation on the same point tires attention; to keep attention alive the object of attention must unceasingly change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When progress stalls, set a new question or change the aspect of the problem to revive interest and avoid wandering thoughts. Use fresh sub-questions to rekindle productive thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foresee and test properties of the result by varying data
rubrics_metrics.description: Varying the data can reveal definite properties the final result must satisfy and thus suggest methods or allow checks of the final formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use limiting cases and boundary values (e.g., b=a and b=0 for frustum) to predict how a correct formula should behave and to test the found result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use auxiliary elements/problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce auxiliary constructions or reduce the original problem to a more accessible auxiliary problem which can be solved and then used to complete the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: construct a diagonal to introduce a triangle when constructing a trapezoid; transforming to a parallelogram leads to a triangle construction with usable data. Auxiliary elements often come from varying or extending the figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify and iterate on unsuccessful trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn from partially successful or unsuccessful attempts by modifying them; a later successful trial may be a refinement of an earlier failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record what was useful in failed trials and adapt it (e.g., first try decreasing c then increasing it in trapezoid example). Avoid discarding first attempts as wholly useless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalog of typical modes for varying a problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain modes of variation are typically useful: introducing auxiliary elements, generalization, definition, decomposing and recombining, specialization, and analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically try these transforms when stuck — e.g., generalize the statement, decompose into parts, seek analogous problems, or specialize parameters to simpler cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher intervention principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A teacher should not ask extraneous questions when a student is progressing spontaneously but should find suitable questions or suggestions when the student gets stuck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow independent work when progress is evident; intervene only to prevent loss of interest or careless mistakes, using targeted questions from the heuristic list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core diagnostic questions about a problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeatedly ask and be able to answer: What is the unknown? What are the data? What is the condition? (For 'problems to prove': What is the hypothesis? What is the conclusion?)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to check understanding and focus attention on principal parts. They can and should be repeated at different phases of the solution and specialized (e.g., list individual data items or condition clauses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right aspect/attack (accessibility principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Success depends on choosing an aspect of the problem that is accessible; to find it, try various sides/aspects and vary the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically probe which approach makes the problem more tractable; this includes changing representation, introducing auxiliaries, or transforming the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of complete proofs for teaching reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete proofs (leaving no gaps) are the best means to acquire the idea of rigorous proof, intuitive evidence, and strict reasoning — especially exemplified by Euclidean geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve place for geometric proofs in education to impart standards of rigorous reasoning and to provide a logical system as a model for other disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry as a logical system
rubrics_metrics.description: A logical system arranges axioms, definitions, and propositions so that each proposition can be based on preceding ones; proofs cement the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with a coherent logical system (like Euclid's) is necessary to take part in debates about rigid logic and to appreciate systematic reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mnemotechnic (memory) role of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs help connect facts and thereby aid memory; simple proofs can serve as effective mnemonic devices for retaining related facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when full logical aims are not pursued, arranging facts with simple connecting proofs or figures (e.g., Fig.23 for triangle angle sum) improves retention compared to isolated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing instruction to a cookbook system
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching procedures without proofs (the 'cookbook') risks delivering unmotivated rules that are quickly forgotten and fail to give coherent understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance practical instruction with reasons; for applied students (e.g., engineers) long epsilon-style proofs may be inappropriate, but removing all reasoning reduces mathematics to recipes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of incomplete proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Incomplete proofs can be useful to lend interest and plausibility or as mnemotechnic devices, but they are not substitutes for complete proofs and must be distinguished from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incomplete proofs to present the main idea/germ and indicate the nature of remaining details; ensure they are clearly marked as incomplete and that the teacher/author knows the full proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for presenting incomplete proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof is incomplete, it must be indicated as such; authors/teachers must know the complete proof themselves and not present an ambiguous half-proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting incomplete proofs with pretension that they are complete. Indicate incompleteness somewhere and ensure appropriate framing so students understand limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proverbs heuristically but skeptically
rubrics_metrics.description: Proverbs capture heuristic procedures and common-sense rules for problem-solving but are often inconsistent and not universally applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and group relevant proverbs for phases of solution but apply them with judgment; do not treat them as authoritative laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the problem fully and desire the solution
rubrics_metrics.description: First do and understand the problem: 'Who understands ill, answers ill.' See clearly the end you must attain and foster a strong desire to solve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think on the end before you begin ('respice finem'). Without clear aim and desire, difficult problems are unlikely to be solved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devising a plan is the main achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceiving an appropriate action or plan is the core accomplishment; persistence, varied means, and adapting trials are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try different methods, adapt trials to circumstances, prepare backup schemes ('have two strings to your bow'), and cultivate the habit of recognizing and using available opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start execution at the right moment and order steps properly
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin carrying out the plan when ripe (not rashly, not hesitating too long) and arrange steps in the proper sequence, which may be the reverse of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use judgment about timing; stepwise verification that details fit the outline. Be aware that the order of discovery may differ from the order of exposition and execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look back and reexamine the completed solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Reexamining the solution can provide additional confirmation; 'second thoughts are best' and having two proofs is safer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After solving, check for alternative proofs, verify steps, and seek further confirmation; looking back is an instructive phase of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working backwards (method of analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visualize the desired final situation clearly, then ask from what antecedent that situation could be derived; discover an appropriate sequence of operations in reverse and then reverse them to execute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Pappus-style analysis: assume the goal achieved and infer predecessors (examples: measuring 6 quarts with 9 and 4 quart pails). Be aware of psychological difficulty in thinking in reverse, but it is a powerful and systematic technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy and induction as sources of conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy and induction often start discovery in mathematics and the sciences; heuristic analogies can frame plausible arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies (e.g., spherical vs rectilinear triangles) tastefully to suggest conjectures; treat such heuristic arguments as plausibility, not as full proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligent trial-and-error vs blind repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial-and-error is normal, but quality of trials matters: vary trials intelligently and explore possibilities rather than mindless repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the 'insect' approach (doing the same hopeless thing); emulate the 'mouse' or 'man' who varies trials and learns. Keep track of what changes and why they might work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use targeted sub-questions to reconquer interest when blocked
rubrics_metrics.description: When progress is blocked, set a new question from the heuristic list to uncover untried contacts with prior knowledge and revive effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pose specific sub-questions (e.g., What are the unknowns? What is the first datum?) to redirect attention and reveal new approaches.
